abstract: Coordinate Network Mapping (CNM) has become an important approach for translating scattered neuroimaging findings into circuit-level models of brain disorders such as Alzheimers disease (AD). But conventional CNM uses fixed-radius spheres and pools heterogeneous studies without accounting for confounders. We developed Global weight-Ranked cluster-grOWing (GROW), which reconstructs clusters behind reported peaks using cluster information and a reference statistical weight map, without original imaging data. We analyzed data from 521 participants and 69 published studies (82 experiments, 5,555 participants). GROW-CNM was compared with fixed-radius CNM (Fixed-CNM) in spatial fidelity, cross-study convergence, sampling stability, and sensitivity to confounders. At study level, Fixed-CNM corresponded poorly with the reference atrophy-derived functional network in AD (Spearman r = -0.24, overlap = 1.61%), and radius changes did not improve fidelity. In contrast, GROW-CNM recovered cluster morphology and generated maps closer to the reference network (r [≥] 0.85, overlap [≥] 87.30%). GROW-CNM also showed greater cross-study convergence (median peak probability, 0.99 vs. 0.67; z = 27.42, p < 0.001) and was robust to threshold/resampling (z = -169.84, p < 0.001). Fixed-CNM was associated with systematic factors; GROW-CNM was more sensitive to demographic confounders (p < 0.05, TFCE-FWE correction). Systematic confounding was attenuated by GROW-CNM; Fixed-CNM remained susceptible in core regions (p < 0.001). These findings indicate cross-study heterogeneity in coordinate-based AD network maps reflects seed definition and study-level confounders, not biology alone. Combining GROW-based seed reconstruction with confounder-adjusted population modeling may provide a robust framework for mapping disease-related brain networks and prioritizing candidate neuromodulation targets.
